relationship: Parallel foreigner defeat and territorial-gain notices

relationship: David's victory and the Euphrates-control clause in parallel accounts
rationale: Both summaries describe David striking a king and mention establishing control at the Euphrates; Hadadezer son of Raab, Zobah and Adraazar, Souba, Hemath remain as supplied, without assigning the final he to a newly resolved actor.

relationship: Matching chariot and foot totals with distinct mounted-force wording
rationale: Both give a thousand chariots and twenty thousand foot soldiers and leave a hundred chariots after disabling the rest; Samuel's seven thousand horsemen and Chronicles' seven thousand horses remain distinct wording rather than an independently reconstructed inventory.

relationship: Damascus reinforcements and the stated twenty-two-thousand strike

relationship: Damascus garrison, gift-bearing service and divine success refrain
rationale: Both report a Syrian garrison near Damascus, service with gifts and the Lord sustaining David's success; victory wherever he went and kept saving in all journeys retain their actual formulations rather than an exhaustive historical verification.

relationship: Gold ornaments brought from enemy servants to Jerusalem
rationale: Both report David taking gold worn by the enemy king's servants and bringing it to Jerusalem; Samuel names armlets and Chronicles collars, without treating those different object labels as independently verified identical artifacts.

relationship: The later Shishak account expressly recalls David's Hadadezer spoils
rationale: Samuel adds that Shishak took the gold spoils in Rehoboam's days; Kings names Shishak's Jerusalem campaign and David's Hadadezer spoils, preserving Samuel's armlets alongside Kings' golden spears and shields without harmonizing their physical object labels.

relationship: David's bronze spoil explicitly linked with Solomon's bronze objects
rationale: Both link David's large bronze haul with Solomon's bronze sea, pillars and vessels; Samuel's additional basins and Masbak and Chronicles' Metabechas remain intact, without independently equating the town forms or every listed object.

relationship: Parallel peace embassies with different names and vessel lists
rationale: Both accounts have a king send his son to bless David after the enemy's defeat and bring vessels; Toi/Ieddouran and Thoa/Idouram remain as supplied, while Samuel's silver, gold and bronze are not reduced to Chronicles' silver and gold.

relationship: Same-chapter dedication heading specified by the following spoil list
rationale: David dedicates the silver and gold with what came from dominated cities; the next unit specifies Idumea, Moab, Ammon's sons, foreigners, Amalek and Hadadezer's spoil, giving the particular scope of that dedication.

relationship: Named enemy groups in the parallel dedication summaries
rationale: Both lists associate dedicated silver and gold with Idumea, Moab, Ammon's sons, foreigners and Amalek; Samuel additionally names Hadadezer's spoil, without silently making the two complete lists identical.

relationship: Eighteen-thousand Idumean notices with different stated actors and places
rationale: Samuel credits David with eighteen thousand in Idumea at Gaimale; Chronicles credits Abessa son of Sarouia with eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salts. The numerical and regional literary parallel does not resolve those different actor and place clauses into one reconstruction.

relationship: Same-chapter garrison-and-service notices reuse the divine victory refrain
rationale: The Idumean garrison, service and Lord-gave-victory notice repeats the earlier Damascus garrison, gift-bearing service and victory wording, retaining the distinct regions and not adding gifts to the Idumean unit.

relationship: David's judgment and righteousness for Israel expressly repeated
rationale: Both summaries say David reigned over Israel and administered judgment and righteousness for all his people, preserving that stated royal assessment without extrapolating approval to every subsequent action.

relationship: Joab's army role repeated beside distinct recorder-parentage forms
rationale: Both administrative lists put Joab over Israel's army and name Jehoshaphat as recorder; Ahia and Ahilud remain the different supplied paternal forms, without independently harmonizing them.

relationship: Zadok's priestly role repeated within different official lists
rationale: Both lists expressly name Zadok among the priests; Samuel8 also names Ahimelech son of Abiathar and Asa as scribe, while the later list has Abiathar and Sousa, so this connection does not reverse parentage or equate all officials.

relationship: Benaiah son of Jehoiada in administrative and service accounts
rationale: Both name Benaiah son of Jehoiada in David's service; the later account reports his deeds and appointment to receive instructions, without replacing counselor or David's sons' palace-official role in the earlier summary.

relationship: Jonathan-house mercy request and David's explicit Jonathan-sake inquiry
rationale: David asks for someone of Saul's house to receive mercy for Jonathan's sake; Jonathan had asked that mercy never be removed from his house or his name from David's house, grounding the particular family connection.

relationship: Same-chapter identification of Ziba prepares his particular family answer
rationale: The Saul-house servant is named Ziba and called before David; the next exchange has Ziba identify Jonathan's surviving son by parentage and injured feet, without giving that son's personal name in this exchange.

relationship: Jonathan's injured son recalled with the same explicit parentage

relationship: Same-chapter stated Machir-house location followed by retrieval from it
rationale: Ziba places the man with Machir son of Ammiel at Lo-debar; the next unit says David brought him from that same named house and location, connecting report and action without mapping the site anew.

relationship: Same-chapter royal retrieval follows Ziba's explicit location report
rationale: David sends to Machir son of Ammiel's house at Lo-debar after Ziba identifies that location; the repeated household designation supplies the particular destination rather than an unreported journey route.

relationship: Mephibosheth explicitly linked through Jonathan to Saul

relationship: Same-chapter promised royal-table provision followed by stated practice

relationship: Mercy for Jonathan's family recalls the earlier household request

relationship: Dead-dog self-description before different royal audiences
rationale: Mephibosheth calls himself a dead dog before David; David had earlier asked Saul whether he was pursuing a dead dog and flea, comparing the speakers' particular self-lowering words rather than assigning that valuation as the narrator's judgment.

relationship: Same-chapter declaration to Ziba recalls the land-restoration promise

relationship: Same-chapter household cultivation command and Ziba's compliance pledge
rationale: David assigns Ziba's family and servants the land work and bread provision while reserving Mephibosheth's royal-table place; Ziba's following answer promises obedience, without treating that pledge as proof of every later harvest.

relationship: Same-chapter royal-table eating explicitly follows the earlier promise
rationale: The narrator says Mephibosheth ate like a king's son at David's table, matching the earlier continual-table promise; Ziba's obedience statement remains his own pledge rather than an independent performance report.

relationship: Same-chapter Ziba's household service beside the earlier work instruction
rationale: The notice says Ziba's whole household served Mephibosheth; the earlier instruction assigns Ziba, his sons and servants the land work, preserving the separate Mica-son notice without adding an unprovided age or land share.

relationship: Same-chapter continued table provision restates the promised benefit
rationale: The ending says Mephibosheth ate continually at the king's table, the benefit David had explicitly promised; his two injured feet remain the supplied personal description without an invented medical explanation.

relationship: Ammonite succession notices in parallel narratives
rationale: Both narratives open with an Ammonite king's death and his son's succession; Hanun and Anan remain the supplied son-name forms, without claiming independent verification of every individual-name equation.

relationship: David's stated filial mercy and condolence mission in parallel accounts
rationale: Both quote David proposing mercy to the new king because the father had shown him mercy and sending comforters; Hanun/Nahash and Anan/Naas remain as supplied, without reconstructing the earlier unreported kindness.

relationship: Same-chapter spying accusation contrasted with David's stated condolence purpose
rationale: The Ammonite leaders allege city inspection and spying; David's preceding speech explicitly proposes mercy and comfort over the father's death, preserving accusation and declared purpose without independently deciding private motives.

relationship: Envoy humiliation with different stated shaving and cloak details
rationale: Both accounts describe shaving David's servants and cutting their cloaks; Samuel explicitly has their beards shaved and cloaks cut in half at the hips, while Chronicles has shaved them and half cloaks to the fold, without adding half-beard wording.

relationship: The explicit Jericho waiting instruction repeated
rationale: Both report David responding to the men's dishonour by telling them to remain in Jericho until their beards grow and then return, preserving that particular instruction rather than an unreported length of stay.

relationship: Same-chapter hired contingents followed by their stated deployment
rationale: The hiring notice names Syrian, Maacah and Istob forces with their counts; the formation notice places the named allied groups in the field and Ammon at the gate, without independently reconciling every Beth-rehob, Rehob and Zobah designation.

relationship: David's dispatch of Joab and the mighty force repeated
rationale: Both accounts say David heard and sent Joab with the whole mighty force, identifying the particular royal response to the Ammonite mobilisation without adding the king personally to that first dispatch.

relationship: Ammon at the city gate and the allies separately in the field
rationale: Both dispositions put Ammon by the city gate and the allied forces separately outside; Samuel names the Syrian groups while Chronicles calls them the arriving kings, retaining those actual descriptions.

relationship: Joab's response to opponents in front and behind
rationale: Both report Joab seeing opponents before and behind and selecting young Israelites to face Syria, preserving the specified tactical choice without a newly drawn battlefield plan.

relationship: The two conditional rescue directions explicitly shared
rationale: Both speeches distinguish Syria prevailing over the speaker from Ammon prevailing over the other force and promise reciprocal rescue, without treating both hypothetical defeats as actual events.

relationship: Courage for the people and God's cities with the same divine-goodness appeal

relationship: Joab's advance followed by Syrian flight in parallel accounts
rationale: Both narrate Joab and his accompanying people advancing or drawing up against Syria and the Syrians fleeing, without resolving every earlier troop count as the number engaged here.

relationship: Ammon's retreat after Syrian flight with distinct opposing-actor clauses
rationale: Both report Ammon entering the city after seeing Syria flee and a return to Jerusalem; Samuel says they flee before Abishai, whereas Chronicles names Joab and Abessa, keeping those actual actor clauses intact.

relationship: Same-chapter defeated Syria regathers before the new reinforcement notice
rationale: Syria regathers after seeing its defeat; the next unit describes Hadadezer gathering forces from beyond Chalamak with Shobach at their head, without assuming every man from the first engagement returned.

relationship: Beyond-river reinforcement notices with distinct river and leader forms
rationale: Both describe additional Syrian forces from beyond a river with a named commander; Samuel's Chalamak, Ailam and Shobach and Chronicles' River and Sophach remain their actual wording without importing an unprovided crossing location.

relationship: David's all-Israel mobilisation and Jordan crossing repeated
rationale: Both say David gathered all Israel, crossed Jordan and met the Syrians arrayed for battle; Samuel additionally names Ailam, without adding that place to Chronicles' shorter account.

relationship: Parallel Syrian outcomes with different counted units and figures
rationale: Samuel reports seven hundred chariots destroyed and forty thousand horsemen killed; Chronicles has seven thousand chariot fighters and forty thousand foot soldiers. Shobach and Sophach remain the supplied leader forms without harmonising the figures or troop classes.

relationship: Changed allegiance and the end of Syrian help with distinct stated procedures
rationale: Both end the defeat account with service to the victors and Syria no longer helping Ammon; Samuel has kings desert to Israel and Chronicles a covenant with David, without inserting the latter procedure into Samuel.

relationship: Royal campaign, Rabbah siege and David remaining in Jerusalem
rationale: Both put Joab's army campaigning against Ammon and besieging Rabbah while David remains in Jerusalem; Chronicles adds Joab striking and razing Rabba, without supplying that final outcome to Samuel's opening notice.

relationship: Same-chapter royal-roof episode situated during David's stated Jerusalem stay

relationship: Same-chapter identified married woman followed by David's taking and intercourse

relationship: Same-chapter intercourse account followed by the woman's pregnancy message

relationship: Same-chapter Joab sends the requested Uriah and the audience occurs
rationale: David requests Uriah from Joab and Joab sends him; the next unit says Uriah arrives and David asks about Joab, the people and the war, recording that particular summons and arrival without inventing Uriah's answers.

relationship: Same-chapter welfare inquiries belong to the ordered military audience

relationship: Same-chapter refusal to go home receives Uriah's stated reason
rationale: Uriah sleeps with the servants at the king's door instead of going home; his later reply places the ark, Israel and Judah in tents and Joab and the servants in the open field, and refuses going home to eat, drink and lie with his wife, preserving his stated reason.

relationship: Same-chapter David's question repeats the reported failure to go home
rationale: David is told Uriah did not go to his house and asks why; the preceding narrator notice states that precise action and alternative sleeping place, without an additional accusation or fabricated answer.

relationship: Same-chapter refusal to go home repeated after the royal meal
rationale: Uriah declares he will not go home to eat, drink and lie with his wife while the force camps; after David makes him drunk he again sleeps with the servants instead of going home, preserving both his speech and the later narrated action.

relationship: Same-chapter promised sending-away followed by the next-morning letter dispatch
rationale: David tells Uriah to remain and says he will send him away; the later morning notice says a letter was sent by Uriah's hand, without independently resolving every interval in the today-and-tomorrow wording.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated sleeping-with-servants outcome despite the changed meal scene
rationale: After David's meal and drunkenness, Uriah still does not go home and lies with the servants; the earlier notice likewise puts him with servants at the king's door, without claiming every detail of the sleeping place is repeated.

relationship: Same-chapter the letter borne by Uriah contains the stated lethal order
rationale: David sends a letter to Joab by Uriah's hand, and the next unit quotes its command for Uriah's exposed position, withdrawal and death; the text does not say Uriah knew or read its contents.

relationship: Same-chapter lethal battle instruction beside the reported placement and death
rationale: The letter orders Uriah placed in fierce fighting and withdrawal behind him; Joab places him where he knows there are powerful men, and the account reports his death, without adding an unreported description of every withdrawal manoeuvre.

relationship: Same-chapter stated placement followed by the city's attack
rationale: Joab puts Uriah where he knows powerful men are; the next unit has city men attack, David's servants fall and Uriah die, linking the particular placement and outcome without inferring every fighter's intent.

relationship: Uriah's narrated battle death explicitly charged to David later
rationale: The battle account says Uriah dies with other servants; Nathan later charges David with killing Uriah by Ammon's sword and taking his wife, retaining the narrator's event and the prophet's assignment of responsibility.

relationship: Same-chapter Joab's report mission followed by the actual messenger audience
rationale: Joab sends the battle report to the king; the later unit says the messenger reaches Jerusalem and tells David what Joab instructed, connecting dispatch and delivery rather than inventing another messenger.

relationship: Same-chapter report instruction introduces the specified anticipated royal response
rationale: Joab instructs the messenger about finishing the battle account; the following units specify a possible angry wall-approach question and the Uriah-death answer, retaining the conditional form at this stage.

relationship: Same-chapter anticipated anger and wall question occur in the actual audience
rationale: Joab's instructions anticipate David asking why the force approached the wall; the later narration explicitly says David becomes angry and repeats the wall question, preserving the source edition's full response.

relationship: The explicit Abimelech-millstone recollection beside the earlier death narrative
rationale: The anticipated question names a woman throwing a millstone fragment onto Abimelech; Judges narrates that blow and then his armour-bearer's sword blow, without making the recalled warning an exhaustive account or resolving Thamasi against Thebez by a new map.

relationship: Same-chapter anticipated Abimelech warning repeated in David's actual speech
rationale: Joab forecasts an Abimelech-and-millstone question before the Uriah report; David's actual audience repeats that question, including Thamasi, without claiming the anticipated quotation alone had already been spoken.

relationship: Same-chapter actual royal speech corresponds to Joab's conditional instructions
rationale: David becomes angry and cites the wall danger and Abimelech after Joab prepared the messenger for those questions, preserving the actual source-edition response rather than omitting its repeated speech.

relationship: Same-chapter the messenger's gate account continues with the wall-shooting losses
rationale: The messenger says the enemy advanced and his force pressed to the gate; his next words report arrows from above the wall and the deaths of servants and Uriah, giving the particular sequence he reports without independently verifying it.

relationship: Same-chapter actual Uriah-death answer matches the instructed concluding report
rationale: The messenger tells David Uriah also died, the exact fact Joab had instructed him to add after the anticipated wall question; the speech is not expanded into an additional undisclosed casualty list.

relationship: Same-chapter David's not-evil instruction contrasted with the Lord's evil assessment
rationale: David tells Joab not to regard the reported battle matter as evil and attributes varied losses to the sword; the chapter closes by calling what David had done evil in the Lord's eyes, contrasting the evil wording while retaining the broader scope of the concluding judgment.

relationship: Same-chapter the wife's mourning follows the reported Uriah death
rationale: Uriah's wife hears he died and mourns him after the messenger's explicit Uriah-death report, without adding an unreported account of who delivered her news or what she knew of the letter.

relationship: Same-chapter the later marriage follows the earlier identification and taking
rationale: The woman becomes David's wife after mourning Uriah; the earlier inquiry identified her as Uriah's wife before David took her, preserving the change of stated marital setting and the Lord's concluding judgment.

relationship: The Nathan-David-Bathsheba setting explicitly named in the psalm heading
rationale: The Lord sends Nathan to David after the Bathsheba episode; Psalm 50's heading explicitly names David and Nathan's coming after he went in to Bathsheba, preserving the source edition's psalm numbering and the heading's own scope.

relationship: Same-chapter plentiful flocks contrasted with refusal to use them
rationale: The rich man has very many flocks and herds, yet the later part of Nathan's story says he refuses his own animals and takes the poor man's lamb, identifying the particular abundance-and-taking contrast within the parable.

relationship: Same-chapter the sole nurtured ewe lamb becomes the stated object taken
rationale: The poor man's only lamb is reared like a daughter, eating and drinking with the household; the following action takes that lamb for the visitor, preserving the particular cherished animal rather than a generic livestock theft.

relationship: Same-chapter the parable's taking action followed by Nathan's direct application
rationale: Nathan's story has the rich man take the poor man's lamb instead of his own resources; Nathan then tells David You are the man who did this, connecting the explicit application without equating every narrative detail to a separately proved event.

relationship: Same-chapter David's death judgment turns toward the addressed king
rationale: David angrily declares the parable's offender deserves death; Nathan answers by identifying David as that man, preserving judgment and application without treating David's spoken penalty as an already executed sentence.

relationship: Sevenfold restitution language in different stated circumstances
rationale: David orders sevenfold repayment for the ewe lamb and lack of pity; Proverbs says a caught thief repays sevenfold and gives possessions, without replacing Samuel's sevenfold with fourfold or asserting that both passages prescribe an identical legal case.

relationship: The royal-anointing reminder beside the actual Samuel anointing
rationale: Nathan's divine message recalls anointing David king over Israel; the earlier narrative names David, the Lord's anointing command and Samuel's oil action, without independently reconstructing every subsequent step of Saul's pursuit.

relationship: The rebuke recalls earlier divine gifts and royal elevation
rationale: The rebuke enumerates the given house, wives and Israel-Judah rule; the earlier divine speech recalled David's movement from sheepfold to rule and God's presence and renown, comparing particular benefaction summaries without inventing an unreported transfer ceremony.

relationship: Nathan's Uriah-killing charge refers to the ordered battle exposure
rationale: Nathan charges David with killing Uriah by Ammon's sword; the earlier letter commands exposed placement and death, followed by the narrated killing, distinguishing David's responsibility from an invented personal sword stroke.

relationship: The wife-taking charge recalls the woman's explicit marital identification
rationale: Nathan says David took Uriah's wife; the earlier inquiry identifies Bathsheba as Uriah's wife and then narrates David sending for and taking her, grounding the particular charge rather than an assumed unrelated marriage.

relationship: The named adultery and murder prohibitions beside Nathan's paired charges
rationale: Nathan charges taking Uriah's wife and killing him; the law expressly forbids adultery and murder, here at Exodus20:13 and20:15 with the theft command between them, preserving the actual source-edition numbering and the prophet's particular charges.

relationship: Announced household sword beside the later stated killing of a royal son
rationale: Nathan announces that the sword will not depart from David's house; the later account has Absalom order Amnon killed and the young men perform that command, offering a particular household episode without claiming an exhaustive proof of the word never.

relationship: Public household-sexual-shame announcement beside the later roof episode
rationale: The announcement concerns David's wives given to a neighbour before the sun; the later account says Absalom entered his father's concubines on the roof before all Israel, preserving wives versus concubines and the actors actually named rather than silently equating every clause.

relationship: The explicit secret-versus-public contrast and the later all-Israel wording
rationale: Nathan contrasts David's secret act with a consequence before all Israel and the sun; the later roof account expressly says before the eyes of all Israel, comparing that particular public wording without adding an unreported mechanism of divine causation.

relationship: David's sin-against-God confession in narrative and psalm
rationale: David says he sinned against the Lord, and the Davidic psalm says Against Thee alone I sinned and did evil before Thee; Nathan's sin-put-away and nondeath reply remains part of the narrative without being inserted into the psalm verse.

relationship: David's repeated explicit sin confession in distinct royal crises
rationale: David tells Nathan he has sinned against the Lord; after the later census he tells the Lord he has sinned greatly and asks removal of lawlessness, preserving the different addressees, occasions and responses that follow.

relationship: Same-chapter stated child-death announcement followed by the reported death
rationale: Nathan says the born son will die despite the assurance that David will not die; the later notice explicitly reports the child's death on the seventh day, without independently defining every detail of the provoked-enemies clause.

relationship: Same-chapter the child's narrated illness follows the particular announced consequence
rationale: After Nathan leaves, the narrator says the Lord struck the child and he became ill; the preceding word announced that child's death, without generalising this episode into an explanation of other children's illnesses.

relationship: Same-chapter fasting for the child receives David's own explanation
rationale: David seeks God, fasts and lies in sackcloth on the ground; he later explains that he fasted and wept while the child lived in hope of mercy, keeping his stated purpose distinct from a guaranteed healing promise.

relationship: Same-chapter refusal to rise or eat contrasted with the later changed response
rationale: David refuses the household elders' attempt to lift him and will not eat; after the death he rises, washes, worships and eats, preserving the particular change of conduct without diagnosing his mental state.

relationship: Same-chapter servants' fear of reporting the death followed by David's direct question
rationale: The servants fear telling David the child died; his noticing their whispers leads him to ask and receive the death confirmation, without asserting that the harmful actions they feared actually occurred.

relationship: Same-chapter whispered knowledge becomes explicit death confirmation
rationale: David perceives the death from the servants' whispering and asks them; the preceding notice gives the event and their reluctance to tell him, without claiming an unreported supernatural disclosure.

relationship: Same-chapter changed eating conduct prompts the servants' question
rationale: David rises, washes, anoints, worships and eats after the death; his servants explicitly ask about the contrast with his earlier fasting, preserving their reported question without adding a ceremonial timetable.

relationship: Same-chapter servants' contrast question and David's actual answer
rationale: The servants ask why fasting ended when the child died; David answers with his prior hope of mercy and the inability to bring the child back, without turning the exchange into an independently elaborated afterlife doctrine.

relationship: Same-chapter hoped-for mercy explains the earlier fast and vigil
rationale: David says he fasted while the child lived because the Lord might have mercy; the earlier narration records his seeking God, fasting and ground vigil, preserving the hope as conditional rather than a promise of recovery.

relationship: Same-chapter irreversible death response follows the reported child's death
rationale: David asks whether he can bring the child back and says he will go to him; the earlier narrative reports the child's death, without supplying an unspoken place, timing or full doctrine for that final clause.

rationale: The source names the son Solomon after David comforts Bathsheba; Chronicles likewise names Solomon in David's Jerusalem offspring, preserving its different Bersabee/Amiel maternal wording without independently equating it with Bathsheba/Eliab.

relationship: Same-chapter the Idedi naming notice follows the Lord's stated love
rationale: The child-naming notice uses Idedi because of the Lord after the statement that the Lord loved Solomon; the unqualified sending and naming pronouns are not independently reassigned, nor is a different name or new etymology supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter the narrated capture is restated with a different city description

relationship: Same-chapter Joab's capture report grounds his explicit request to David
rationale: Joab reports taking the city of waters and asks David to gather the rest and capture the city first, retaining the actual repeated first wording without independently harmonising every capture notice.

rationale: Joab asks David to gather the remaining people, encamp and capture the city; the next unit explicitly has David gather the people, go to Rabbah, fight and capture it, without adding a new motive beyond Joab's named concern.

relationship: Same-chapter David's reported capture follows Joab's particular appeal
rationale: David gathers the people and captures Rabbah after Joab requested his arrival to prevent the city being named for Joab, without cancelling the separately worded earlier Joab capture notices.

relationship: Royal crown, talent of gold and precious stone in parallel spoil accounts
rationale: Both describe the opposing king's crown, a talent of gold and precious stone, its placement on David's head and great city spoil; Melchol and Molchol remain their supplied forms without replacing the king with a newly identified god or interpreting the weight as a bodily measurement.
